To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the anomalously long distances of sorbing radonuclides in fractured crystalline rock can be explained by the sparse distribution of chemially reactive grains in the rock matrix.

the sparse distribution of chemologically reactive grains is the main reason for the anomalously high cesium penetration profiles, and that the medium can be described as a composite system with most of the radionuclide mass being retained close by the injection boundary and the rest being transported along preferential diffusional pathways.
the spatial distribution of sorbing mineral phases is the most important control on the diffusivity of sorbing nuclides in a crystalline rock matrix.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new generation of reactive transport models, which are able to capture the complex behaviour of the fractured crystalline rock matrix, in terms of its heterogeneous structure and the distribution of reactive grains.
the development of a new approach to simulate reactive transport in fractured crystalline rock.

the development of a new approach to model radionuclide transport and retention in fractured crystalline rock, which takes into account the heterogeneity in the spatial distribution of chemically active minerals, as observed in the laboratory and in-situ experiments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the anomalously long penetration profiles observed in in-situ experiments are not due to the existence of a large population of very reactive grains, as previously suggested, but rather to the sparse distribution of chemi- cally reactive grains.

the Inter-Granular model, with a realistic description of the spatial distribution and properties of the chemically reactive grains, is capable of capturing the key features of the diffusion of sorbing radions in fractured granitic rocks.
the sorbing radionusclides are not transported by a single diffusive pathway but rather by two parallel diffusive paths, with one being fast and the other slow.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Inter-Granular Model, based on the micro characterisation data and the grain-scale description, provides a plausible explanation for long distance diffusion of radionuclids in fractured crystalline rock.
the observed anomalous diffusive patterns are a direct consequence of the spatial distribution and connectivity of the reactive grains.

the observed long-distance transport of sorbing radionsuclides in crystalline rock can be explained by a simple model based on a two-pathway diffusion process, which is in turn controlled by the sparse distribution of reactive grains in the rock matrix.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in fractured crystalline rock, the sorbing radionusclide diffusion and sorbtion can be strongly controlled by the spatial distribution of reactive grains, which can be described by an Inter-Granular network model.

the spatial distribution of sorbing mineral grains, which can be easily obtained using modern micro tomographic techniques, can be directly incorporated into reactive transport codes in order to obtain realistic predictions for sorbing radonuclide migration in fractured crystalline rock.

the spatial distribution of chemically active grains in a granitic matrix is an important control on the diffusivity of sorbing radonuclides and needs to be accounted for in the modelling of the transport of these radionuclids in the rock matrix.
